text:
Evidence-grounded evaluation offers a useful bridge from rejection narratives to measurable diagnostics. [FActScore (2023)](https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.741.pdf) decomposes generated text into atomic claims and measures source support; [ALCE (2023)](https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.398.pdf) separately evaluates correctness and citation quality, with metrics correlated with human judgments. Applied here, each proposed rejection reason should include a supporting history event or title/description span, its timestamp where relevant, and a supported/contradicted/insufficient-evidence label. These papers validate grounding methods, not the ability to recover actual rejection reasons from implicit interactions.

Recommended adaptation: distinguish observable repetition or explicit specification conflicts from unknown personal fit. Similar titles can indicate content overlap, but do not establish ownership, unwanted redundancy, device ownership, mood, or current intent. Recent interactions provide temporal context rather than proof of a present need. Annotate item facts separately from user-fit claims; abstain when the latter lack evidence. [Research on self-explanation faithfulness (2024)](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.19/) finds reliability depends on the explanation, model, and task, supporting independent verification rather than accepting fluent rationales.

For calibration, have independent human annotators label a stratified sample using only permitted evidence; report per-reason precision/recall, inter-annotator agreement, unsupported-claim rate, and precision versus coverage under abstention. Include lexical-overlap baselines, paraphrases, and high-overlap examples with conflicting specifications to test whether probes detect meaning. Treat these as proposed controls requiring local validation. Without explicit user rejection feedback, the resulting labels measure evidence-supported failure hypotheses, not confirmed reasons for rejection.
